doc.title: Wilson "Chembo" Corniel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

title: The unplanned improvised moment in yesterday's demonstration
summary: The ensemble must be together before improvising; communication between players cannot be planned.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: There was a great moment when I think you’d been talking about how someone asked a question about how much improvisation is involved in most of the things. And the answer was that not as much as you might think. And then you played one of the rhythms and Victor at one point gave this big smile. He looked at you guys, and obviously you had just done something a little out of the ordinary, which I’m assuming was improvised. So what is my question. I’m not sure I have a question, except it was very noticeable.

Okay well the answer is that you know he might have done something, he said a conversation was just playing then loudly I answered him back, I communicated back with him like it was a give and take kind of thing and this is what it’s about you know. If I was improvising because I was doing the solo parts on the quinto on the congas and he was playing his parts there, and when everybody is — first of all the ensemble has to be there first of all, together. Because we have to play where we’re not fighting each other, we’re laying a bed first so you can lay on top and relax and do what you want to do, but the conversation and the ensemble part has to be together first before you go to the next step as far as your improvisation. Okay? So when he probably heard some communication between us or between us three somewhere, that it was in time because this is what we play for and this is through experience you get it. You know? Because you can’t say okay let’s talk first and you do this first. You can’t plan that. This is what

improvisation is. You can’t plan it. I’m hearing you say [garbled speech] so it’s got — or I might do a riff and then you might do the same rhythmically, like on your solo, you could be blowing and I can do a little [scats] you know then you can answer me back to give you something to grab onto, to communicate back with me. Like I hear you. So I think this is one of those moments that we strive to look for, when it’s not planned.
